title_zh: 第二十三類 法術騙

stories.title_en: A Monk Uses a Mirror Trick to Plot Rebellion

paragraphs.en: Among the arts of monks there is one that works by chanting spells over water. The monk secretly casts the spell on a man, and whatever that man longs for in his heart, when he is then told to look into the water himself, his own image appears in it accordingly. There was a man named Mi Chunyuan, worth over a million, whose fields stretched across two prefectures. He was past fifty and no longer thought of sitting the metropolitan examination; his only pleasure was living in ease and luxury. A sorcerer-monk heard of his wealth and schemed to cheat him out of a rich profit. Wielding the water-charming art, he went and knocked at Mi's gate, claiming that he could read the aura of a place: every time he passed this residence, he said, he saw purple vapors rising into the sky, shot through with the colors of the phoenix and the luan. This was an omen of kings and marquises for a hundred generations; someone here was destined to perform great service in upholding the dynasty's fortune and to receive a fief under an everlasting oath of enfeoffment. Mi Chunyuan did not believe him. The monk said, "I hold a secret transmitted art: with talismans and enchanted water one can learn the rise and fall of this life and how it will end. A man need only fast for three days and come to look with a devout heart, and whatever he is meant to achieve in this life will appear of itself in the water." Mi then took the monk in and ordered everyone in the household to fast.

On the third day, they filled a great vat with water in the courtyard. The monk muttered spells over the water in secret and had each person look into it in turn. Mi looked and saw himself wearing a Y-shaped celestial crown and a python robe. His youngest son saw the same. The two elder sons saw only gauze caps and round-collared robes. Mi's principal wife saw a consort's crown and a phoenix robe. The two elder daughters-in-law saw only pearl crowns and pheasant-plumed gowns. Mi was astonished but kept it locked in his heart.

Later, at a banquet with a certain Zhi, a former official residing there, the talk turned to current affairs. Zhi said, "As things stand, the rivals are evenly matched, and the stakes rest on the cadet line. The first sprout of calamity will surely arise within the palace. One day, there will be either a bloodbath like Emperor Chengzu's seizure of the throne, or a call to revolt from a princely house like the Prince of Yi's. This is precisely what the widow of Lu deeply feared." Mi said, "In the past, rebellion was crushed before it could take root, and Chenhao was destroyed as soon as he rose. The dynasty enjoys Heaven's favor—how could wind and rain shake its doors?" Zhi replied, "Not so. Liu Wenjing, a minor official, set the Tang uprising in motion; Yao Guangxiao, a monk, helped raise an emperor's house. Once a cause finds capable men to back it, who can predict success or failure?" Mi said, "Even if the central plains fall into turmoil, our watery region lies far off in a corner by the sea; surely we need not fear chaos here." Zhi said, "That too is hard to guarantee. A prophecy says, 'A Son of Heaven shall emerge from a certain place, and Jiangnan shall become a battlefield.' That is precisely what we must fear." Mi asked, "If Chenhao were to rise again today, how would it end?" Zhi said, "The realm has been at peace so long that the troops have grown slack—even worse than in those days. Had Chenhao not lingered so long at Nankang, and had a certain garrison not feigned allegiance only to turn their spears against him, how would his grand enterprise have gone up in smoke?" Upon hearing this, Mi felt secretly delighted.

There was another monk who could call down a spirit to possess a boy, and it spoke of coming fortunes and misfortunes like an echo answering a sound. Mi asked him to call the spirit down, and prayed in secret about his plan to commit treason. The spirit descended and said: "The golden bell rises, the jade aura waxes; pure fortune upholds the king, the imperial enterprise grows strong. A mighty flood sweeps the land clean and the people rest in peace; carve up the soil, move the palace, and hold the far frontier." Mi still could not tell whether this boded good or ill, and begged for a plainer answer. The possessed boy shouted, "What manner of thing is this, that you dare babble on about it!" Mi dared not ask again, and still did not grasp the spirit's meaning. Soon afterward a fisherman hauled a huge bell out of a deep pool, gleaming gold. Mi took it as an auspicious sign. He summoned Zhi and the two monks to settle their plans for revolt: they would wait for a certain day in the fifth month, at dawn, when officials high and low would all leave the city to send off the emperor's birthday memorial; then they would shut the four gates, station troops in ambush outside the walls, and slaughter them to a man.

At the fourth watch, the soldiers on duty rose early and noticed unusual lights and fires at the places where the ambush troops were hidden inside the city. They rushed a report to the officers, who called out troops to make arrests. The city fell into commotion, and more soldiers were sent to man the walls. From the walls they saw countless boats on the river, all cooking an early meal. Suspecting they had come to aid the revolt, the soldiers on the wall shouted, "So-and-so plotted treason—he has been caught and beheaded!" The men in ambush outside saw no signal cannon from within, saw that the walls were manned, and heard the shouting; the officials escorting the memorial never came out of the city. Knowing the plot must have been exposed, the several dozen boats along the river scattered and fled in the first faint light. Later the authorities treated the rioters as having plotted rebellion and an attempt to rob the treasury; several dozen men were captured, and all were beheaded. But the ringleader pleaded that he had known nothing of it; he was sentenced only to exile three thousand li, and died on the road.

Note: Provincial Graduate Mi was old and enormously rich; he had long lost any ambition for higher civil office, so why would he dream of becoming a king or a prince? It was only that the water-spelling sorcerer monk stirred the notion, the spirit-channeling monk hardened his resolve, and the cashiered official Zhi nursed resentments until treason was brewed. The two monks were executed, while Zhi narrowly slipped through the net. Men of this age who are seduced by sorcerer monks into treasonous plots may take this as a warning.

stories.title_en: Sorcerers Send a Dream, Then Plunder the House

paragraphs.en: Old foxes hide in rocky caves by day and come out at night to feed on the fruits of grasses and trees. If one happens to breathe in the generative essence of heaven and earth among the plants, it gains spiritual powers: it can transform into a beautiful woman to bewitch and seduce men, draining their yang essence to increase its own magic. When a ritual master catches such a fox and cooks it, a monk who manages to obtain the fox's heart roasts it dry, fumes it with fine incense, builds a thatched hut deep in the mountains, and enshrines the heart inside. By day he chants every kind of penitential text and sutra to deliver its soul; by night, hordes of demons and monsters—howling, calling, moaning, weeping, shrieking, whistling, some speaking human words, some barbarian tongues, in a thousand uncanny shapes—come to mourn outside the hut, a scene of utter desolation. It takes a man of extraordinary nerve to dare stay inside. After seven days of mourning, the visitors gradually thin out. Day and night he keeps chanting sutras and performing rites, laying out fruit and food as offerings. When forty-nine days have passed, he burns the hut down, takes the fox heart home, and keeps it on an altar with incense. If he means to call on someone the next day, the night before he puts the fox heart in a brocade pouch and lays it over his own heart. That night he is sure to dream of a woman who leads him to meet the man. The next day, when he goes to pay his respects, the man has already met him in a dream. Afterward, whatever he asks for, people find it uncanny and usually grant it. This is one of the tricks monks use to swindle and convert others.

There was a rich man named Old Yang, who had two sons and two daughters-in-law. His savings were ample, yet he was a terrible miser, unwilling to give away even a single cash coin in charity. One night he suddenly dreamed that two eminent monks came begging for alms. The next day, two monks arrived exactly as they had appeared in his dream. They said, "You have been too grasping in gathering wealth, and much resentment has built up against you. We share a bond with you from a former life and have come especially to perform repentance on your behalf." Old Yang believed them and asked, "How should the repentance be done?" The monks replied, "Your whole household must fast for three days. Then buy fruit, cakes, pastries, and the three sacrificial meats—pork and mutton—half meat and half vegetarian. We will perform rites for you, summon spirit generals, chant sutras, and make offerings to the Buddha to absolve your lifetime sins. Then we will pray for increased fortune and emolument hereafter, so that your household enjoys good luck and after death you escape falling into perdition." Old Yang did as they said, fasting and buying the provisions.

On the third day two more monks arrived, and they too were kept on to help chant the sutras. That evening one monk chanted spells and burned talismans, and set Old Yang jumping and shouting under a spell. Yang snatched up a sharp sword, pointed at his wife and sons, and cried, "These are demons!"—and cut them all down with his own hand. Then he chased after the two daughters-in-law to kill them. The women begged the monks to restrain him. A monk pointed at Old Yang and barked, "Sit!" Sword in hand and teeth clenched, Yang sank into a dazed stupor, dead to the world. The four monks went in, raped the two women one after another, and bound them with ropes. They ransacked the house for money and valuables, tied the loot into four carrying loads, and fled in the dead of night.

The next day, someone entered the house and found Old Yang with his hair loose, crouched over a sword, eyes open and muttering. He rushed out and called for others to come look. Relatives and neighbors poured in. Old Yang kept saying he had to kill demons. They stepped forward, wrested the sword away, and called him by name: "What has happened to you?" Little by little, Old Yang came around. When they questioned him again, he finally answered: "I dreamed there were many demons here, and I was killing them—until you called me awake." When they went into the back rooms, his wife and children had all been killed. Old Yang wailed, "That much I remember: I killed three demons here, then chased two demon-women to kill them too, but the monks held me off." When they went into the inner room, both women were tied up on the beds. They called in neighbor women to free them. Each said she had been raped by the monks, and that all the gold, silver, and valuables had been gathered up and carried off. The household's grief and hatred knew no end. While they laid out the three corpses for burial, they also sent men chasing the monks on every road; the pursuers traveled two days' distance, saw no trace of them, and returned.

Note: Old Yang was naturally stingy, so he had indeed committed acts of heartlessness befitting a rich man. Yet when the monks frightened him with talk of resentment, he believed their words and kept them on to perform blessings and repentance—because his conscience was already guilty. The monks intended to use magic to rob him, revealing themselves first in a dream; this was the fox-heart art of inducing dreams put to use. He dreamed they were eminent monks, yet they turned out to be robber monks. To disbelieve what happens by daylight but believe what is dreamed at night is delusion; to do no good in ordinary times yet seek repentance through fasting is folly. Nowadays many people are cruel and heartless, greedy and unjust, yet hope to feed monks and make offerings to the Buddha, buying repentance after the fact. How are they any different from Old Yang in his ruin? It is beyond measure: evil must not be done, and monks are not to be trusted. Let this example make you shudder.

stories.title_en: The Face-Rubbing Swindler Who Abducts Young Children

paragraphs.en: Some years ago, young boys in the capital who went out were sometimes kidnapped and carried off, with searches turning up no trace. Later it happened again and again. Many people had seen a monk stroke a boy's face, whereupon the boy would follow him away; when they went looking soon after, the boy was already gone. Thus the capital buzzed with talk of a "cheek-rubbing rogue." At that time there were many monks in the capital, and no one could tell which one it was.

A wealthy man surnamed Mi had only one son who went out and never returned. The family searched frantically in every direction and posted reward notices everywhere: "Twenty taels of silver to anyone sheltering him; ten taels for information." They put up notices and offered rewards all around, but never learned his whereabouts.

A man named Ban Ba, who lived in a small house on the Mi property, made his living scavenging the streets. One day, too lazy to go scavenging, he wandered out to Huizhen Hermitage outside the city for a stroll, turned into the rear quarters, and poked around on every side. Suddenly a small boy's head showed through a broken slatted screen. Ban Ba recognized him as the Mi family's son and called out at once, "Your family is searching everywhere for you—what are you doing here?" The Mi boy said, "The monk has me locked up in here. Come rescue me, quick!" Ban Ba saw that the door was locked. Afraid he could not get the boy out alone, he told him, "Stay put and keep quiet for now. I will report to your father and come straight back for you." He ran home at full speed and told Old Mi, "Your son is being held in Huizhen Hermitage. Go rescue him at once." Old Mi immediately rounded up fifty-odd men, who converged on the hermitage from front and back. Ban Ba led them to the back room, broke the door open, and picked out the Mi boy; a search turned up a dozen more boys. He had the men bind the monk Xiaoshan and the three others of the hermitage, and they were all trussed up and delivered to the authorities with a formal complaint.

The magistrate first interrogated the children: "How were you lured into the hermitage?" The boys replied, "The monk rubbed our eyes with his hands, and immediately we saw fierce tigers and venomous snakes on both flanks and behind us, lunging to bite and harm us. Only a single clear path lay open before us, so we kept running forward until we reached this hermitage, where the monk locked us away." The magistrate asked again, "What did the monk keep you here to do?" The boys said, "That hateful monk—day and night without end, he forced us to suffer his abuse, causing excruciating pain. If anyone refused, he thrashed us with heavy staves. Terrified of him, we had no choice but to submit to whatever he did." The magistrate asked further, "Those kidnapped earlier must have grown older—where were they sent?" The boys said, "Whenever any grew sick or grew older, the monk claimed he was letting them go home, but we do not know whether any ever made it back." The magistrate then interrogated the monk Xiaoshan: "After kidnapping these boys, where did you send those who fell sick or grew older?" The monk dared not answer. When the magistrate questioned the other three monks of the hermitage, all three confessed: "They were poisoned to death and buried." Hearing this, the magistrate was seized with furious indignation. He had Xiaoshan given forty strokes of the cane and each of his three accomplices given twenty, declaring: "For a crime so heinous, even death is too light a punishment!" He ordered Xiaoshan chained outside the yamen gate and permitted the parents of the missing boys to assemble and beat him together. They struck him until he was broken and bleeding, and within half a day he perished. There was no one who did not detest his villainy and rejoice at his death. Later the authorities burned the hermitage to ashes, and the scourge of child abduction was finally brought to an end.

Note: A taste for boys is the conduct of beasts. This monk must have had some aphrodisiac formula; without kidnapping young boys he had no way to glut his lust. He had also learned a sorcerer's art: a rub over their eyes made their sight blur and showed them terrors, so he could lure the boys away. His crimes rose higher than the sky. When his measure of evil was full, the crowd did the killing. To speak of it shames the tongue; to write of it soils the page. Who would not gnash his teeth at it? Any man with a male body—how could he follow in this monk's evil ways?
